attacker_pocs.name: newbug
attacker_pocs.why: A self-recursive pattern (?P<x>a(?&x)?b) drives internal_dfa_match() to recurse via OP_RECURSE until the base workspace is exhausted; with pcre2_set_heap_limit(mctx,2) in force, the OP_RECURSE frame (ovecsize == RWS_OVEC_RSIZE) calls more_workspace() on the heap-capped path. The patched fallback sizes the block with RWS_OVEC_OSIZE instead of the requested ovecsize, so the 1008-int block is far too small for the RWS_OVEC_RSIZE ovector plus RWS_RSIZE workspace; the recursive call's workspace[0]=0 write (pcre2_dfa_match.c:696) lands ~2000 ints past the end -> ASan heap-buffer-overflow. On the parent, more_workspace() returns PCRE2_ERROR_HEAPLIMIT (-63) for the same input, so nothing is written out of bounds.

role_a_rationale: Task completed: more_workspace() now checks rws->next->size >= RWS_RSIZE+ovecsize+RWS_ANCHOR_SIZE before reusing a chained next block, which is the documented fix for GHSA-3r4p-g7gg-ppmf (reuse of a too-small next workspace block); the stale-next pointer is preserved (new->next = rws->next) so cleanup still frees the whole chain, and the full RunTest suite passes under ASan with no regression. New defect: on the heap-limited allocation path, when the doubled/capped size is below the required minimum the code falls back to newsize = RWS_RSIZE + RWS_OVEC_OSIZE + RWS_ANCHOR_SIZE, hardcoding the small assertion-ovector constant instead of the per-call ovecsize. For an OP_RECURSE frame (ovecsize == RWS_OVEC_RSIZE) this block is undersized by ~2000 ints, and the recursive internal_dfa_match() writes its workspace out of bounds. The change looks mergeable: it reads as a reasonable 'fall back to a minimum-sized block instead of failing' refinement using an existing named constant, and the error-return is still present for the truly-exhausted case; the bug is only visible once one notices ovecsize varies between OSIZE and RSIZE call sites. The parent is secure for this input (returns PCRE2_ERROR_HEAPLIMIT), so the defect is genuinely new to the changed code.
